mission: LawAI provides legal research and advice for AI policy through three teams: US Law & Policy, EU Law (including the AI Act's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice) and Legal Frontiers, which develops new ideas like 'Law-Following AI'. It also trains lawyers through fellowships.

key_work.title: Law-Following AI: Designing AI Agents to Obey Human Laws
key_work.plain_summary: Argues AI agents should be built to refuse illegal actions even when instructed, and explains how law could require this.

key_work.title: Treaty-Following AI
key_work.plain_summary: Extends the law-following idea to international agreements: AI systems designed to respect treaties between states.

key_work.title: Automated Compliance and the Regulation of AI
key_work.plain_summary: Explores how AI itself could cut the cost of complying with AI rules, changing how regulation should be designed.

key_work.title: Architectures of Global AI Governance (book)
key_work.plain_summary: Matthijs Maas's book mapping the options for international institutions to govern AI.

key_work.title: Cambridge Commentary on EU General-Purpose AI Law
key_work.plain_summary: A legal commentary explaining the EU AI Act's rules for general-purpose AI models clause by clause.

warnings.text: Policymakers often lack the legal expertise to write effective AI regulation.
AI agents may take actions that break the law unless designed and regulated not to.
If AI developers create risks, the public may bear the costs unless liability rules make developers responsible.

recommendations.text: Require AI agents to follow the law ('law-following AI').
Use liability and insurance so developers bear responsibility for the risks they create.
Build mandatory AI incident reporting (e.g. under the EU AI Act and California law).
Do not let AI developers hire their own referees — use independent assessment.
